sketches.title: Thanks, I Guess
sketches.premise: You have to write a thank-you note for a gift nobody wanted. Turn the awkward little fact on the card into a wildly overconfident note without losing what actually happened. The host will admire your gratitude, then inspect it for lies.
sketches.criterion: The note must still make clear that the named giver gave the named unwanted thing to the named receiver.
sketches.move_shape: Write a thank-you note under 90 characters, including a greeting or sign-off, that keeps the card's fact true; for example, card: "Mia gave Tom a broken mug" → "Dear Mia—your broken mug completes my museum of bad choices. Love, Tom."
sketches.first_card: Ben gave Ava a singing birthday card that would not stop.

sketches.title: Sorry About the Gift
sketches.premise: A thank-you note nobody wanted to write becomes an apology nobody asked for. You must thank the giver while making the unwanted gift sound like the cause of a tiny personal disaster. The host scores the distance between the plain fact and your excuse-riddled masterpiece.
sketches.criterion: The note must still show that the receiver got the stated gift from the stated giver and is thanking that giver for it.
sketches.move_shape: Write one apologetic thank-you note under 90 characters, with a reason for the apology; for example, card: "Leo gave Priya a loud toy" → "Thanks, Leo—sorry the toy taught my dog three new swear words."
sketches.first_card: Nora gave Sam a hat that was two sizes too small.

sketches.title: Dear Customer Service
sketches.premise: Pretend the thank-you note is a complaint filed with the universe. Keep the gift and giver intact, but describe the present like a product that has ruined your life, your home, or possibly civilization. The host checks the receipt, because apparently manners need paperwork.
sketches.criterion: The entry must clearly identify the named giver, receiver, and gift, while remaining recognizably a thank-you note.
sketches.move_shape: Write a fake customer-service thank-you under 90 characters; for example, card: "Ella gave Max a cactus" → "Thanks, Ella. Cactus arrived sharp, hostile, and exactly as advertised."
sketches.first_card: Kai gave Jo a glitter-covered notebook.

sketches.title: Thanks for the Trauma
sketches.premise: Turn the unwanted thank-you note into a message sent to the wrong family group chat. The card's small truth must survive, while your version may add witnesses, grudges, secrets, and one relative who should absolutely not be replying. The host is judging the note, not your family’s need for therapy.
sketches.criterion: The message must still state that the giver gave the receiver the specified unwanted gift and that the receiver acknowledges it with thanks.
sketches.move_shape: Write a group-chat-style thank-you under 90 characters, using at least one reply, tag, or reaction; for example, card: "Owen gave Lily a frog toy" → "Thanks, Owen. @Mum says the frog stays out of her bed this time."
sketches.first_card: Tess gave Ray a book about frogs.

sketches.title: A Statement to the Press
sketches.premise: Your thank-you note has become a public statement after the unwanted gift causes a scandal. Thank the giver, preserve the boring truth, and spin the object into evidence of triumph, corruption, or a suspiciously cheap cover-up. The host will ask whether your statement still knows what gift it got.
sketches.criterion: The statement must still make the giver, receiver, gift, and act of thanking unmistakably true.
sketches.move_shape: Write a press-style thank-you under 90 characters, sounding like a public official; for example, card: "Rosa gave Dan a tiny trophy" → "Dan thanks Rosa for the tiny trophy; an inquiry into its missing base begins."
sketches.first_card: Maya gave Eli a medal made of plastic.

sketches.title: The Final Polite Words
sketches.premise: Write a thank-you note as if it is the last polite message before a friendship, wedding, job, or civilization ends. You may threaten, flirt, roast, or confess, but the gift must remain the gift and the thank-you must remain real. The host rewards the biggest leap from manners to mayhem without letting the note quietly change the facts.
sketches.criterion: The note must still truthfully thank the named giver for giving the named unwanted gift to the named receiver.
sketches.move_shape: Write a dramatic final thank-you under 90 characters; for example, card: "Ned gave Bea a rubber duck" → "Thanks for the duck, Ned; when the ship sinks, I’ll remember your betrayal."
sketches.first_card: Ivy gave Cal a mug with Cal’s face printed on it.
